title: Thread-pool starvation
sub: The server doesn't crash, it crawls
cards/0/body:
ASP.NET Core has no context, so .Result won't hang. But every such request holds a pool thread while it waits for the database. How much that hurts depends on how the pool adds threads:

  • up to the MinThreads threshold (by default, the number of cores) the pool creates threads immediately, on demand;
  • beyond the threshold, cautiously. If a thread is blocked by something the pool can't see (Thread.Sleep, synchronous I/O, lock), the pool checks every half second whether the queue is moving and adds one thread at a time;
  • blocking on .Result and .Wait() the pool notices by itself since .NET 6: it immediately adds as many extra threads as there are cores, and after that waits before each new one, from 25 ms up to 250 ms.

You can raise the threshold with ThreadPool.SetMinThreads.
cards/0/deep: Beyond MinThreads, the thread count is tuned by the hill-climbing algorithm: it tries slightly more or slightly fewer threads and watches whether throughput improves. The half-second check is a safety net for when the queue stalls. Blocking behavior is tunable through the System.Threading.ThreadPool.Blocking.* settings in runtimeconfig.json.
cards/1/body:
Step by step: 8 cores, 100 requests with .Result arrive.

  • 1. 8 threads take 8 requests and block on .Result. The pool sees the blocking and immediately adds 8 more, which take the next requests and block too. The other 84 wait in the pool's queue.
  • 2. The database responses arrive. But the continuations that the blocked threads need go into the same queue, behind the new requests.
  • 3. New threads now arrive with delays, and a new thread often picks up not a continuation but the next request, which blocks on .Result as well.
  • 4. There are dozens of threads now, responses stretch to seconds, and the CPU is almost idle.

If the blocking comes from Thread.Sleep or a synchronous read instead of .Result, the pool doesn't see it and adds threads even more slowly, one every half second.
cards/2/task: Add 16 requests with .Result and start the clock. How many threads are stuck, and how does the pool grow?
cards/3/task: Now the same 16 requests, but with await.
cards/4/q: 16 requests with .Result bloated the pool, while the same 16 requests with await were served by 4 threads. Why?
cards/4/options/0: With .Result a thread is stuck for the whole database wait; with await it's free while we wait and takes the next piece of work
cards/4/options/1: With await the database answers faster
cards/4/options/2: The pool knew in advance the requests were asynchronous and decided not to add threads
cards/4/explain: Waiting without a thread is the main benefit of async on a server. The pool doesn't need more threads because none of them is stuck.
cards/5/q: Under load, responses lag by seconds while the CPU is nearly idle. What do you suspect first?
cards/5/explain: An idle CPU with growing latency means the threads exist, but they're stuck.
cards/6/body: In dotnet-counters, watch the pool's queue length and its thread count. A growing queue and a thread count that creeps upward while CPU load stays low is a sure sign.
cards/6/deep: On .NET 8 these are the ThreadPool Queue Length and ThreadPool Thread Count counters; since .NET 9, the dotnet.thread_pool.queue.length and dotnet.thread_pool.thread.count metrics. In a process dump (dotnet-dump), starvation shows up as dozens or hundreds of threads whose stacks end in .Result or Wait.
cards/7/q: What can cause thread-pool starvation? Select all that apply.
cards/7/options/0: .Result and .Wait() on tasks that query the database
cards/7/options/1: Thread.Sleep in code that runs on the pool
cards/7/options/2: A synchronous read from a slow disk in every request
cards/7/explain: Anything that holds a pool thread without doing work.
cards/8/q: A quick "fix": ThreadPool.SetMinThreads(500, 500). What do you say?
cards/8/options/0: It hides the symptom: more threads at once, but they sit idle just the same; the cure is switching to await
cards/8/options/1: Great fix: blocking costs nothing anymore
cards/8/options/2: It will speed up the database
cards/8/explain: The MinThreads threshold removes the delay in growing the pool, not the blocking. Hundreds of waiting threads mean memory and context switches. The real cure is not to block.
